about: Sourced life story for Jesus. Written from Scripture: the KJV text of the four Gospels and Acts, told Gospel by Gospel; events ordered by the site's Gospel harmony (A. T. Robertson's order).

jesus-isa-7-14.short: Jesus of Nazareth, whom the Gospels call the Christ, the Son of God; born of Mary, he taught and healed, was crucified, and rose from the dead.

paragraphs.text: Matthew and Luke tell of his birth: Matthew of Joseph's dream, the wise men and the flight into Egypt; Luke of the angel's visit to Mary, the shepherds and the manger. In Matthew, Mary, espoused to Joseph, was found with child "of the Holy Ghost", and an angel told Joseph in a dream to call the child JESUS, "for he shall save his people from their sins"; Matthew says this fulfilled the prophet's words, "Behold, a virgin shall be with child". Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea "in the days of Herod the king", and wise men came from the east asking for the one "born King of the Jews"; they found the young child with Mary his mother, worshipped him, and gave him gold, frankincense and myrrh. Told by an angel in a dream, Joseph took the child and his mother into Egypt, and Herod killed the children of Bethlehem "from two years old and under". After Herod died Joseph brought them back into the land of Israel, and they lived "in a city called Nazareth".

Luke tells that the angel Gabriel was sent to Nazareth, to a virgin named Mary who was espoused to Joseph, to tell her that she would bear a son, "and shalt call his name JESUS"; he "shall be called the Son of the Highest". Mary answered, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." A decree of Caesar Augustus took Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, "the city of David", where she laid her firstborn son in a manger, "because there was no room for them in the inn", and an angel told shepherds in the same country, "unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord." When he was brought to the temple to be presented to the Lord, Simeon took him in his arms and said, "mine eyes have seen thy salvation". At twelve years old, at the Passover, he stayed behind in Jerusalem and was found in the temple "sitting in the midst of the doctors", and said, "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"; then he went home to Nazareth, "was subject unto them", and "increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man".

Mark begins his Gospel, "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God", with John the Baptist. Matthew and Mark tell how Jesus was baptized by John in the Jordan, and Luke that he was baptized "when all the people were baptized"; in Matthew, John at first forbade him, saying, "I have need to be baptized of thee". In all three the heavens were opened, the Spirit came down upon him like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, in Matthew, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased", and in Mark and Luke, "Thou art my beloved Son". John's Gospel does not tell the baptism itself, but there John the Baptist says, "I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove", and calls Jesus "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world". Then he was forty days in the wilderness, "tempted of Satan", as Mark says; Matthew and Luke tell of three temptations by the devil, in a different order, and to the first Jesus answered, in Matthew's words, "It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone".

John's Gospel tells that two of John the Baptist's disciples followed Jesus, and that one of them, Andrew, told his brother Simon, "We have found the Messias". Matthew and Mark tell how, by the sea of Galilee, Jesus called Simon and Andrew to be "fishers of men", and then called James and John. After John was put in prison, Mark says, Jesus came into Galilee "preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God"; Luke tells how at Nazareth, "where he had been brought up", he read from the prophet Esaias in the synagogue and said, "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears", and the people thrust him out of the city. Mark records the people of his own country asking, "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon?" Out of his disciples he chose twelve, "whom also he named apostles", Luke says, after a night in prayer.

Matthew says he went about all Galilee "teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness". In Matthew 5 to 7 he teaches his disciples on a mountain, beginning "Blessed are the poor in spirit" and giving the prayer "Our Father which art in heaven"; at the end the people "were astonished at his doctrine: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes". Luke gives a sermon spoken when he came down and "stood in the plain", beginning "Blessed be ye poor". Much of his teaching was in parables: Mark says "without a parable spake he not unto them", and Matthew gives "the parable of the sower" with others told from a ship by the sea. Luke alone tells the parables of the Samaritan who had compassion on a man left half dead, and of the younger son whose father said, "this my son was dead, and is alive again".

Matthew, Mark and Luke speak of his "mighty works". All three tell of a leper made clean at his touch, of a man sick of the palsy told to "Arise" and go to his house (Mark says he had been let down through the roof, Luke "through the tiling"), and of devils cast out; in Mark, after word came that the daughter of Jairus was dead, he took her by the hand and said, "Damsel, I say unto thee, arise". When he rebuked the winds and the sea, the men in the ship marvelled, in Matthew's words, "What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him!" All four Gospels tell how he fed about five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, and Luke alone tells of a widow's son raised at Nain. In Matthew, when John the Baptist sent from prison to ask, "Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?", Jesus answered, "The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up".

John begins, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God", and says, "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us". He calls the water made wine at a marriage in Cana "this beginning of miracles", by which Jesus "manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him". John tells of several visits to Jerusalem at the feasts; at a Passover near the start of his account Jesus drove the sellers and the changers of money out of the temple, while Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of him casting out the sellers after he rode into Jerusalem, near the end of their accounts. Nicodemus, "a ruler of the Jews", came to him by night and heard, "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God"; and at Jacob's well, when a woman of Samaria spoke of the Messias who was to come, Jesus told her, "I that speak unto thee am he".

In John, Jesus speaks of himself in sayings that begin "I am": "I am the bread of life", "I am the light of the world", "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep", "I am the way, the truth, and the life". When he said, "Before Abraham was, I am", they took up stones to cast at him. John tells that when Lazarus of Bethany had lain in the grave four days, Jesus said to his sister Martha, "I am the resurrection, and the life", wept, and cried, "Lazarus, come forth", and the dead man came out. From that day, John says, the chief priests and Pharisees "took counsel together for to put him to death". John writes that Jesus did "many other signs" not written in his book, "But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God".

He asked his disciples, "But whom say ye that I am?" (near Caesarea Philippi, Matthew and Mark say). Peter answered, in Matthew, "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God"; in Mark, "Thou art the Christ"; in Luke, "The Christ of God". From that time, Matthew says, Jesus began to show them "that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day", and all three tell how he said it again on the way. Some days later he took Peter, James and John up a mountain, where he was transfigured before them and Moses and Elias talked with him, of "his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem", Luke says; and a voice from the cloud said, in Mark and Luke, "This is my beloved Son: hear him". Mark records his words, "the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many", and John his saying, "I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me", which signified, John says, "what death he should die".

As the Passover drew near he rode into Jerusalem on a colt (Matthew tells of an ass and her colt); Matthew says this fulfilled the prophet's word, and John that it was as it is written: "thy King cometh". In Matthew and Mark the crowds spread their garments in the way and cried, "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord"; in John they took "branches of palm trees". He cast out of the temple those who sold and bought, saying, as Matthew gives it, "My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves", and Luke says he "taught daily in the temple". The chief priests and scribes, Mark says, "sought how they might destroy him", and Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went to them; Matthew says "they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver".

Matthew, Mark and Luke tell that he ate the Passover with the twelve. In Matthew and Mark, as they ate he said that one of them would betray him; then he took bread and said, "Take, eat; this is my body", and gave them the cup: in Matthew's words, "this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins". Luke tells it in his own order, and adds, "this do in remembrance of me". John does not tell of the bread and the cup; he tells that Jesus washed his disciples' feet, gave a sop to Judas, who "went immediately out: and it was night", and said, "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another". John alone gives the long words he spoke to his disciples before he went out to the garden, and his prayer, "Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son".

In Gethsemane, as Matthew and Mark name the place, he took Peter, James and John apart and prayed, in Matthew's words, "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt"; Luke adds that "his sweat was as it were great drops of blood". Judas came with an armed company sent by the chief priests; in Matthew and Mark he kissed Jesus, and in John, when Jesus said "I am he", they "went backward, and fell to the ground"; and Matthew and Mark say that all the disciples "forsook him, and fled". John says he was led first to Annas and then to Caiaphas the high priest; in Mark, when the high priest asked, "Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?", Jesus said, "I am", and the council condemned him "to be guilty of death". Meanwhile Peter three times denied knowing him, and in the morning they delivered Jesus to Pilate. Pilate's page tells the hearing Gospel by Gospel, until Pilate released Barabbas and delivered Jesus to be crucified.

In Matthew, Mark and John the soldiers put a crown of thorns on his head and mocked him, "Hail, King of the Jews!" Matthew, Mark and Luke tell that Simon of Cyrene was made to bear his cross, and John that "he bearing his cross went forth"; they crucified him at "the place of a skull", Golgotha, which Luke calls Calvary, with two others, one on either side, under a writing that named him King of the Jews. Luke records his words, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do", his promise to one of the two, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise", and, just before he gave up the ghost, "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit". Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of darkness from the sixth hour to the ninth, and Matthew and Mark record that at the ninth hour he cried, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" John records his words to his mother and to the disciple whom he loved, "Woman, behold thy son!" and "Behold thy mother!", then "I thirst" and "It is finished", after which "he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost".

Matthew, Mark and Luke tell that the veil of the temple was rent, and that the centurion said, in Matthew, "Truly this was the Son of God", in Mark, "Truly this man was the Son of God", and in Luke, "Certainly this was a righteous man". John tells that a soldier pierced his side with a spear, "and forthwith came there out blood and water". All four tell that Joseph of Arimathaea asked Pilate for the body and wrapped it in linen; Matthew, Mark and Luke say he laid it in a sepulchre hewn out of rock, and John says it was "a new sepulchre" in a garden, and adds that Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus by night, brought "a mixture of myrrh and aloes". Women who had followed him from Galilee, among them Mary Magdalene, saw where he was laid, and Matthew tells that the chief priests and Pharisees had the stone sealed and a watch set.

All four Gospels tell that on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb, and each tells what followed in its own way. In Matthew, an angel rolled back the stone and told her and "the other Mary", "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said"; Jesus met them as they went, and afterwards met the eleven on a mountain in Galilee and told them, "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations". In Mark, a young man in white told the women, "he is risen; he is not here", and Mark's closing verses say he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, then to two of them as they walked into the country, then to the eleven. In Luke, two men in shining garments asked, "Why seek ye the living among the dead?"; that day he walked unrecognised with two of them to Emmaus and "was known of them in breaking of bread", and then stood among the eleven and those with them in Jerusalem and said, "handle me, and see". In John, Mary Magdalene was weeping at the tomb when Jesus spoke her name; he came to the disciples behind shut doors, eight days later Thomas saw him and said, "My Lord and my God", and he showed himself again by the sea of Tiberias.

At the end of Luke's Gospel he led the disciples out as far as to Bethany, "lifted up his hands, and blessed them", and "while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven"; they returned to Jerusalem "with great joy". Mark's closing verses say that he "was received up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God". Acts says he showed himself alive to the apostles, "being seen of them forty days", and that as they watched "he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight". Two men in white apparel then told them, "this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven".
